titre: Aboard the Space Station, Gravity Has Not Disappeared
accroche: At 250 miles (400 km), gravity is still 88.8% of what it is on the ground. Astronauts float because they are falling with their station, around the Earth.
contenu_vulgarise:
The astronauts aboard the space station float, and they are said to be in “weightlessness,” as if gravity stopped above the atmosphere. NASA says so bluntly on its page on microgravity: many people wrongly think that gravity does not exist in space.

## Almost the Same Gravity

The orbital altitudes of crewed flights range from 120 to 360 miles (about 190 to 580 kilometers) above the surface. At 250 miles, or about 400 kilometers, the Earth's gravitational field is 88.8% of its value on the ground.

A person attracted to the Earth with a force of 700 newtons on the ground is therefore still attracted with about 620 newtons at this altitude, by a simple product. The station does not float in a region without gravity. It stays in orbit there precisely because gravity holds it.

## Falling Around the Earth

If an astronaut lets go of an apple in the station, NASA says, it falls too. You cannot see it fall because the apple, the astronaut, and the station fall together. They fall toward the Earth, but their speed makes them keep missing it: they fall around it. Since everything in the station falls at the same rate, objects seem to float.

This continuous fall is the one Newton imagines. In *De mundi systemate* (published in 1728, after his death), he throws a stone from the top of a high mountain: the faster it leaves, the farther it goes before falling back. At the right speed, the fall becomes a complete circuit, an orbit. For the station, NASA gives 17,500 miles per hour, or 28,000 kilometers per hour.

Gravity has therefore not disappeared. What disappears is the sensation of weight: an object in free fall or in orbit is said to be weightless, and would set a scale to “0” without its mass changing. NASA prefers to speak of microgravity, on the order of 10⁻⁶ g, rather than zero gravity.

## A Fall Without an Orbit

The same situation exists at the surface. In the drop tower at NASA's Glenn center, a shaft of about 500 feet (more than 150 meters) where test packages fall in a vacuum, a little over five seconds of weightlessness are obtained. NASA notes that such facilities are sometimes mistaken for antigravity chambers. According to NASA, roller coasters, a trampoline, or a hilly road give the same effect, in far briefer form.

You do not get rid of gravity by going up. At the station's altitude, nearly 90% of the ground's attraction remains; what the astronaut lacks is a floor to feel it.

What becomes of the fall of an object launched even faster than 28,000 kilometers per hour?

repere.texte: The Earth's gravitational field at about 250 miles of altitude is 88.8% of its value at the surface. An object in orbit falls continuously around the Earth, at 17,500 miles per hour (28,000 km/h) for the space station.

carte.punch: In orbit, gravity is still 88.8% of what it is on the ground. The astronaut is just falling.
carte.idee: At 250 miles (400 km), the Earth's gravity keeps 88.8% of its value on the ground. The astronaut, the apple, and the station fall together, around the Earth, at 28,000 km/h. They float relative to one another; they are not outside gravity.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The page also describes the parabolic-flight aircraft and drop towers used to reproduce weightlessness.

quiz.question: Why do the astronauts aboard the space station float?
choix: Gravity is almost zero at 400 km of altitude
The vacuum of space removes the weight of objects
The station's speed exactly cancels the Earth's attraction
They and the station fall together around the Earth, at the same rate
quiz.explication: At about 250 miles, gravity is still 88.8% of what it is on the ground, so it is not almost zero, and it is not the vacuum that removes weight. The speed of 28,000 km/h does not cancel the attraction: it makes the fall go around the Earth instead of reaching it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: At what speed must the space station travel to stay in orbit, according to NASA?
choix: About 28,000 kilometers per hour (17,500 miles per hour)
About 9,800 kilometers per hour, the Moon's speed
About 100,000 kilometers per hour, to escape gravity
The station needs no speed; it stays suspended
quiz_supplementaire.explication: NASA gives 17,500 miles per hour, or about 28,000 kilometers per hour, the speed that turns the station's fall into an orbit around the Earth.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which thought experiment imagined by Newton sheds light on the principle of orbit?
choix: An apple falling from a tree in his garden
A bucket of water spinning on itself
A stone thrown from the top of a high mountain
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In De mundi systemate, Newton imagines a stone thrown from a high mountain: the faster it leaves, the farther it goes before falling back, until it goes all the way around the Earth.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is obtained in the drop tower at NASA's Glenn center?
choix: Totally zero gravity for an hour
A little over five seconds of weightlessness
An acceleration greater than that of the space station
The exact weight of an object in permanent weightlessness
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The drop tower, a shaft of more than 150 meters where packages fall in a vacuum, gives a little over five seconds of weightlessness, not an hour or permanent weightlessness.
